A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same study of social-impact evaluation reporting. Their complete main texts, appendices, tables, equations and figures are readable and support reliable comparison.

before.justification: v1 reports original annotation and statistical analyses of 186 release-time reports and 183 post-release sources, complemented by ten stakeholder interviews.

after.justification: v2 reports updated analyses covering 248 post-release sources, retains the interviews, and adds original annotation-agreement and statistical sensitivity results.

M1.justification: The scoring framework and principal hierarchical ordinal model are retained. Appendix L.2 adds fitted sensitivity variants with category-specific annotator intercepts and item-category effects, providing limited extensions to the statistical model rather than replacing the central method.

E1.justification: Both versions examine foundation-model reporting across the same seven social-impact categories, provider regions, sectors and stakeholder groups. Additional reporting sources enlarge the sample within this coverage; no distinct new task, domain or target population is established.

E2.justification: Neither version evaluates competing algorithms against a proposed algorithm. The first-party/third-party and organizational comparison groups remain; the added regression variants are sensitivity checks of the study's own analysis.

E3.justification: Post-release sources increase from 183 to 248. The new reliability assessment independently double-annotates 20 release-time models across seven categories and 250 post-release items, adding a substantial validation design. Reported interview duration changes from approximately 30 minutes to 45–90 minutes, without establishing that interviews were repeated.

E4.justification: v2 adds checks using tighter priors, provider-level slopes, and annotator/item effects, testing dependence on modeling assumptions and annotation disagreement (Tables 11–12 and Appendix L.2). Appendix E also expands provider-specific release trajectories beyond v1's Google and Meta examples.

E5.justification: v1 explicitly reports no formal inter-annotator agreement. v2 adds ordinal Krippendorff's alpha, detailed disagreement rates, uncertainty for annotator/item variation, and leave-one-out model comparison with a standard error. Existing Bayesian interval reporting and the eight-chain, 4,000-warm-up/4,000-sampling configuration are retained.

E6.justification: Section 5's first-/third-party means change from 0.72/2.62 to 0.77/2.64, and labor-reporting prevalence changes from 12.12% to 8.06%. The openness–environment coefficient's reported 95% interval changes from [0.009, 1.414] to [-0.065, 1.280], now including zero (v1 Table 3; v2 Table 9). Numerous counts and coefficients are updated, and agreement, sensitivity and detailed provider results are added. These are revised analyses, not same-setting performance gains.

T1.justification: Appendix L.2 introduces mathematical specifications for annotator and item-category effects, assuming zero-mean normal distributions with separate variances. The principal likelihood, hierarchical constraints, time effects and prior equations otherwise remain equivalent despite renumbering; no theorem or proof is added.

C1.justification: The central empirical claims and three stated contributions remain. The abstract strengthens its policy recommendation from policies that promote developer transparency to policies that mandate it, a limited substantive change in the proposed response.

C2.justification: v2 interprets annotation disagreement as substantially item-specific, expands regional recruitment limitations, and adds concrete risks of superficial compliance, exclusionary evaluations and disproportionate reporting burdens on smaller or Global South developers. Existing explanations involving incentives, resources and disclosure barriers remain.

D1.justification: v2 newly documents search dates, screening counts and flow, annotator backgrounds, adjudication, cross-document scoring, ethics approval and interview-quote selection. Some earlier inclusion details are omitted, including the stated 2024-onward search restriction, without establishing an actual change in implementation. Code and dataset links remain the same.

R1.justification: v2 adds Raji et al. (2022) on third-party oversight, Selbst (2021) on institutional incentives, and several model-usage studies; Hobbhahn (2025) is removed. The principal positioning relative to the Foundation Model Transparency Index and Solaiman et al.'s taxonomy remains unchanged.

P1.justification: The abstract and substantial portions of the main-text prose and interview quotations are condensed or rewritten. Terminological footnotes become Appendix A, the appendix hierarchy is reorganized, and separate conflict-of-interest, impact, acknowledgement and author-contribution sections are introduced.

P2.justification: The main text and references change from single-column to two-column layout, and sector/region figures move to the appendix. v2 adds a category overview table, provider-by-release panels, summary-statistics tables, a source-selection flowchart and sensitivity tables, substantially changing the presentation beyond numerical updates or renumbering.

improvement.justification: v2 addresses an important weakness in v1: unquantified reliability of the subjective annotations underlying its conclusions. Agreement testing on 390 independently double-annotated items and sensitivity checks involving priors, provider slopes and annotator/item effects substantially strengthen the evidential basis. Screening documentation also improves traceability. These gains outweigh remaining inconsistencies, including Section 5's outdated academia coefficient of 1.53 versus Table 9's 1.348 and unresolved citations in Appendix G.
